title: Now I see (John 9:13–41)
hookLine: the healed man is questioned, thrown out, and found again by Jesus

cards: A miracle ought to end in a party. A man blind from birth can see. Instead, chapter nine becomes a courtroom drama.

The neighbors argue about whether it's even him: some say yes, others say no, he just looks like him. And the man keeps saying, I am he. Then he's brought to the religious leaders, and the questions start.
How did this happen? Who did it? On the sabbath?
The man who was blind is about to be questioned three times, and he gets braver each time.

teach.h: HE PUT CLAY ON MY EYES.
teach.b: The first time, he just tells the facts: he put clay on my eyes, I washed, and I see. The leaders are divided. Some say a man who heals on the sabbath can't be from God.
Others ask how a sinner could do such signs. What do you think? He's a prophet, the man says.
Then they call his parents, who, frightened, say only: this is our son, and he was born blind. How he sees, we don't know. Ask him; he's of age.

John says they were afraid of being put out of the synagogue. Some readers think this detail also reflects John's own time, when followers of Jesus and other Jewish communities were painfully parting ways.
The man is called back and pressed: we know this man is a sinner.
He answers: "whether he be a sinner or no, I know not: one thing I know, that, whereas I was blind, now I see." He doesn't try to win the theology argument. He stands on the one thing he's sure of.
Then he even gets cheeky: why hear it again? Will ye also be his disciples? And they throw him out.

teach.h: WHEREAS I WAS BLIND, NOW I SEE.
teach.b: Here's the turn: "Jesus heard that they had cast him out; and when he had found him," he asks: do you believe in the Son of man? Who is he, Lord? You've seen him; he's talking with you.
"Lord, I believe. And he worshipped him." Thrown out by one door, he's found by the one who came looking.

how: Christians often share testimonies, simple accounts of what God has done in their lives, and the healed man's "one thing I know" is a common model; the hymn Amazing Grace echoes his words.

games.q: you've been questioned twice. they insist the man who healed you is a sinner. what do you say?
o: "I don't know about that; I know I was blind, and now I see."
games.why: "whether he be a sinner or no, I know not: one thing I know, that, whereas I was blind, now I see."

practice: Let the big questions you can't answer be there, unresolved: about God, about suffering, about what happens next.
Then find one thing you know from your own life, a time you were helped, a change in you, a moment of beauty you can't explain away, and hold it simply, without arguing for it.
If you pray, give thanks for it; if you don't, let it be solid ground.

wordCard.voice: Synagogue. What the healed man's parents feared being cast out of, for saying too much about who healed him.

orig.note: Greek: I see. The healed man's last word in his well-known answer.

carryVoice: Your line: one thing I know. You don't need every answer to say it. Day six hundred eighteen.
